questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Cerebrum: blood supply, internal capsule, basal ganglia, cerebellum
questions.stem: Occlusion of the middle cerebral artery characteristically causes:
options: Contralateral hemiparesis affecting face and arm more than leg, with aphasia if dominant
questions.concept: The MCA supplies the lateral surface including the motor and sensory cortex for face and upper limb and the language areas. The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface affecting the leg predominantly.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Cerebrum: blood supply, internal capsule, basal ganglia, cerebellum
questions.stem: The commonest site of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage is:
options: The putamen, from rupture of lenticulostriate arteries
questions.concept: Lenticulostriate branches of the MCA are called the arteries of cerebral haemorrhage. Because the internal capsule lies adjacent, a small bleed causes dense contralateral hemiplegia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Cerebrum: blood supply, internal capsule, basal ganglia, cerebellum
questions.stem: The posterior limb of the internal capsule carries:
options: Corticospinal fibres, with sensory radiations posteriorly
questions.concept: The compact arrangement of descending motor fibres means a small capsular lacune produces a dense pure motor hemiplegia involving face, arm and leg equally - unlike cortical strokes which are patchy.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Cerebrum: blood supply, internal capsule, basal ganglia, cerebellum
questions.stem: Broca aphasia results from a lesion in:
options: The inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere
questions.concept: Broca area produces non-fluent effortful speech with preserved comprehension and awareness of the deficit. Wernicke aphasia from the superior temporal gyrus gives fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Cerebrum: blood supply, internal capsule, basal ganglia, cerebellum
questions.stem: The circle of Willis is completed posteriorly by:
options: The posterior communicating arteries linking internal carotid to posterior cerebral
questions.concept: Berry aneurysms arise at branch points, most commonly at the anterior communicating artery, then the posterior communicating artery where rupture or expansion causes a painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Cerebrum: blood supply, internal capsule, basal ganglia, cerebellum
questions.stem: A cerebellar hemisphere lesion produces signs that are:
questions.concept: Because cerebellar output decussates twice, signs are ipsilateral - intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, nystagmus, dysmetria and hypotonia. Vermis lesions instead cause truncal ataxia with a wide-based gait.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Cerebrum: blood supply, internal capsule, basal ganglia, cerebellum
questions.stem: The basal ganglia lesion causing hemiballismus is in the:
questions.concept: Loss of subthalamic excitatory drive to the globus pallidus internus disinhibits the thalamus, producing violent flinging limb movements, usually from a lacunar infarct in a hypertensive elderly patient.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Cerebrum: blood supply, internal capsule, basal ganglia, cerebellum
questions.stem: The blood supply of the internal capsule is chiefly from:
options: Lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery
questions.concept: These are end arteries without effective anastomoses, so occlusion produces lacunar infarcts. Their perpendicular origin from a high-pressure vessel also predisposes to Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Cerebrum: blood supply, internal capsule, basal ganglia, cerebellum
questions.stem: Wallenberg (lateral medullary) syndrome results from occlusion of:
options: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery or vertebral artery
questions.concept: It causes ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss, Horner syndrome, ataxia and bulbar palsy with contralateral body pain and temperature loss - a crossed sensory pattern with characteristically preserved motor power.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Cerebrum: blood supply, internal capsule, basal ganglia, cerebellum
questions.stem: Uncal herniation compresses which structure first, producing an early sign?
options: The oculomotor nerve, causing an ipsilateral dilated pupil
questions.concept: Superficial parasympathetic fibres are compressed first giving a fixed dilated pupil, followed by ptosis and a down-and-out eye, then contralateral hemiparesis and finally decerebration.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: General embryology & histology: fertilisation, placenta, epithelia
questions.stem: Fertilisation normally occurs in:
options: The ampulla of the uterine tube
questions.concept: The zygote takes about 3 to 4 days to reach the uterus and implants around day 6 to 7. Delay in transit predisposes to tubal ectopic pregnancy, the commonest site being the ampulla.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: General embryology & histology: fertilisation, placenta, epithelia
questions.stem: Implantation normally occurs in:
options: The upper posterior wall of the uterine body
questions.concept: Implantation in the lower segment produces placenta praevia with painless antepartum haemorrhage. Normal implantation occurs around day 6 to 7 at the blastocyst stage.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: General embryology & histology: fertilisation, placenta, epithelia
questions.stem: The fetal component of the placenta is derived from:
questions.concept: The maternal component is the decidua basalis. Chorionic villi bathed in maternal blood in the intervillous space permit exchange without mixing of the two circulations.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: General embryology & histology: fertilisation, placenta, epithelia
questions.stem: The umbilical cord normally contains:
questions.concept: The vein carries oxygenated blood to the fetus. A single umbilical artery occurs in about 1% of births and is associated with congenital anomalies, warranting careful fetal assessment.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: General embryology & histology: fertilisation, placenta, epithelia
questions.stem: The period of greatest teratogenic susceptibility is:
options: Weeks 3 to 8 of gestation, the period of organogenesis
questions.concept: Before week 3 the all-or-none phenomenon operates. After week 8 teratogens cause functional and growth defects rather than gross structural anomalies, with the brain remaining vulnerable throughout.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: General embryology & histology: fertilisation, placenta, epithelia
questions.stem: Simple squamous epithelium lining blood vessels is termed:
questions.concept: Mesothelium lines serous cavities such as pleura, pericardium and peritoneum, and urothelium (transitional epithelium) lines the urinary tract, allowing distension without loss of the permeability barrier.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: General embryology & histology: fertilisation, placenta, epithelia
questions.stem: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells lines:
questions.concept: Cilia beat mucus towards the pharynx forming the mucociliary escalator, impaired by smoking and absent in primary ciliary dyskinesia, which causes bronchiectasis and situs inversus.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: General embryology & histology: fertilisation, placenta, epithelia
questions.stem: The neural crest gives rise to all EXCEPT:
questions.concept: Neural crest derivatives include melanocytes, sensory and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla, and facial bones and cartilage. The anterior pituitary derives from Rathke pouch, an ectodermal outpouching of the stomodeum.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: General embryology & histology: fertilisation, placenta, epithelia
questions.stem: Meckel diverticulum results from persistence of:
questions.concept: Persistence of the urachus instead gives a urachal fistula from the bladder to the umbilicus, and a patent processus vaginalis gives congenital hernia or hydrocele.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: General embryology & histology: fertilisation, placenta, epithelia
questions.stem: Metaplasia is best defined as:
options: Reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type by another
questions.concept: Barrett oesophagus is columnar metaplasia from acid reflux, and bronchial squamous metaplasia follows smoking. Persistence of the stimulus can lead to dysplasia and then carcinoma.
